newsitem.title: USA: Republicans say Social Security concern unfounded.
newsitem.headline: Republicans say Social Security concern unfounded.

text.p: Republicans Monday accused Democrats of using the popular Social Security system as political cover for votes against the balanced budget amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch, R-Utah, called a news conference to counter Democratic charges that Social Security's retirement benefits would be jeopardized if his party succeeded in passing the balanced budget amendment.

"Talk about a gimmick," Hatch said. "This is a phony issue. It has been exploited for the last ten years," he said, adding that opponents were raising fears about solvency of the retirement fund as a way to kill the balanced budget amendment on the Senate floor later this week.

He remained optimistic that it would pass, although Democratic leaders put its chances at fifty-fifty and an influential House Republican urged Senate leaders to hold off the final vote because support was weak.
"There is no argument against this, except that you want to spend more, you want to tax more," Hatch said later on the Senate floor.

"Only in Washington, D.C., only in this god-forsaken town ... do people believe a $107 billion deficit for a fiscal year is wonderful," he added. Republicans said the Social Security system, which will begin to run deficits around 2019, will be better off if the budget is balanced and the economy improves than if deficits continue to grow.

Republicans have made the balanced budget amendment their number one political goal this year and thought chances of passage were excellent after November's election produced a larger Republican majority and more Democrats supporters.

Now, passage hangs on the decisions of two freshmen Democratic senators, Mary Landrieu of Louisiana and Robert Torricelli of New Jersey who have supported the balanced budget amendment concept. Sometime this week they are to declare which way they will vote.
Democrats are one vote shy of defeating it in the Senate and a House vote has been postponed indefinitely as support for a change to protect Social Security gained momentum even among Republicans.
House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich, R-Ohio, said he doubted Senate Republicans had the votes now to pass the amendment. Republican leaders did not respond publicly to his suggestion.
Sen. Harry Reid, D-Nev., charged Republicans aimed to use balanced budget amendment as a wedge to start cutting Social Security benefits in the next century.
"It will enshrine in the constitution stealing all these monies," he said at the news conference with Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, D-S.D.

The Senate will vote Tuesday on Reid's amendment to exempt Social Security from the deficit calculation. Several other amendments to permit exceptions during economic downturns or for other reasons will considered later in the week.

The balanced budget amendment requires the government balance its budget annually starting in 2002 or when it is ratified by 38 of 50 states. It must pass the House and Senate by two-thirds majority vote. It would not bar red ink but would make it more difficult for Congress to approve deficit spending, higher taxes and borrowing.
